title: Make Masks: magnifier, measurements and reversible editing
description: Inspect the live magnifier, measure paired images and masks with FEATURES, edit real downloaded labels, create a recoverable training crop and review a local detection that disagrees with the existing mask.
objectives: Open paired two-dimensional images and instance masks without modifying the downloaded source.
Preview the Otsu magnifier and measure two real image-mask pairs through FEATURES.
Use reversible object deletion, drawing, division and area filtering, and distinguish these from display contrast.
Save a curated mask and recrop a field while retaining its parent in the recovery archive.
Find nested segmentation tools and inspect a real local Cellpose detection, probability map and flow view.
prerequisite: Obtain Measure's real downloadable example first. The recording uses two isolated TIFF pairs extracted without changing pixels from its seven-plane uint16 merged fields: ER intensity plane 1 and cell-label plane 4. The exact preparation recipe is prepare_fields in tools/tutorials/capture_make_masks.py. For your own experiment, supply two-dimensional images with same-stem instance-label TIFFs in the masks subfolder; do not assume every dataset has this example's plane order.

scenes.narration: Open Make Masks in Home's Tools category. This is the manual mask editor, distinct from the Core Mask pipeline. Its toolbar edits the current field; its header opens related segmentation workflows that live under this parent.

This example uses two real fields from Measure's downloaded dataset. We extracted the intensity and existing cell-label planes into separate TIFF copies and kept the original stacks unchanged. The preparation recipe records their source planes and hashes. Other datasets may use a different plane order.

Open the image folder. Matching instance masks live in its masks subfolder, under the corresponding image stem. The first field loads sixty-three labelled objects. A missing companion starts empty; a label image uses object identifiers, not merely a foreground colour.

The live Magnifier previews segmentation under the pointer. Here its mode is Otsu and its scope is Region under the mouse. This preview uses thresholding on the CPU, without running the Cellpose model.
Turn on Magnifier and hover over the image to inspect its enlarged result. A click would add the outlined objects to the mask. We only hover, then turn it off, leaving the image and labels unchanged.

Features opens the measurement table. We use two real fields, one intensity channel and cell masks. Automatic filename matching may leave files unassigned; add field rows and choose the image and its matching mask explicitly.
Choose each ER image in Channel 1 and the same-stem label image in Cell mask. Repeat for the second field. These are the source images and masks, not screenshots of the coloured overlay.

Check both field rows and their image-mask pairing. Nothing was left over confirms the manual assignments; the earlier regex counter above remains stale. For this demonstration we set one worker, minimum cell size one, and disable saved PNG crops before pressing Measure.

The completed run writes measurements.db for both fields. It contains one hundred and fourteen cell rows with distinct field identities. Every saved area and mean raw ER intensity matches its source label and pixels. Close Features to return to reversible editing.

Brush and Erase work on pixels, while Erase object removes a complete label. Wand controls grow connected intensity regions. Draw, Divide, Zoom and Recrop share this toolbar. Choose the operation that matches the mistake, and inspect the result before saving it.

Click Erase object, then an interior cell. The real click removes exactly label seventeen, changing the count from sixty-three to sixty-two without touching other labels. This is a demonstration of the operation, not a judgment that this cell should be excluded biologically.

Undo restores every original label pixel. Redo repeats that same deletion; Undo restores it again before we continue. These are actual history steps from the clicks, not masks swapped into the viewer by the recording script.

Draw closes and fills an outline as one object. Here a small background outline demonstrates the tool, briefly producing a sixty-fourth label. It is not a biological annotation, and we undo it. Trace a real boundary carefully when preparing training labels.

Divide cuts across an existing object and assigns a new identifier to the separated piece. Start and finish the gesture on the image and cross the whole object. This real cut produces sixty-four labels; we undo it rather than treating a demonstration split as ground truth.

Display percentiles change visibility, not the raw intensities or label geometry. Raising the lower percentile visibly changes this rendering while both arrays remain identical. Restoring it restores the display. Contrast is a viewing aid, not a way to alter the measurements.

The editor's object filter does change labels. Here the measured demonstration threshold of twenty-one thousand and twenty-two pixels removes thirty-two objects when Filter is pressed. No model reruns. This threshold is not a recommended biological cutoff, and this action is not merely hiding objects.

Undo the filter and set its bounds back to zero, which disables them for later fields. Save mask writes the restored labels and their curation record. We verify that its foreground geometry is unchanged; preserve source images separately from the masks you curate.

The header provides Train Cellpose and Mask the whole folder. Training and applying a model are different tasks, with existing specialist lessons linked here. Make Masks remains their parent in the tutorial's Submodules section, even when a tool opens its own window.

The same header contains Model Compare, Model Zoo, Curate and Open in napari. Use their retained lessons for side-by-side model inspection, available weights, curation and the external-editor round trip. We show their actual locations here without repeating or inventing those workflows.

Recrop changes the training field, not just the zoom. Drag a box around a complete object. This gesture immediately writes a new image and matching mask, keeping the original intensity pixels. Labels cut by the boundary are dropped; inspect the resulting object count, not just the box.

Next opens the new one-object crop and retires the copied parent into recropped_originals. That recovery folder preserves its image bytes. This affects the editor's folder queue; it does not rebuild Annotate's crop database. Here only our private tutorial copy is archived, never the downloaded source.

Cellpose-SAM can detect objects in the open field. Our small crop uses cpsam, normalization on, cell-probability threshold zero, flow threshold zero point four and diameter zero, which leaves the model's default sizing. The replacement mode matters: it is different from adding detections to existing labels.

Press Object detection and inspect the result. This CPU run finds one object in the three-hundred-and-thirty-two by two-hundred-and-sixty-seven pixel crop. It outlines the partial object at the upper left instead of the central cell in our existing mask. A matching object count does not mean the segmentation is correct; we will undo this replacement.

Cell probability shows the actual score map from that detection, not a calibrated probability that the biological interpretation is correct. Use it to understand where the model supports foreground. A changed detection threshold requires another detection; these panes describe the run that produced them.

Flows displays the model's directional information. The flow-consistency threshold has a different meaning from the foreground score threshold: lower values are stricter, while zero disables that check. Inspect masks and intermediate views together instead of assuming a larger number always gives a better segmentation.

Undo restores the crop's pre-detection labels without changing its image. Cellpose uses local model weights, not a chat-provider response. The application's device resolver supports available acceleration and a CPU fallback; the options depend on the installation, so do not promise identical results across backends.

For scripts, the editor's load_image_and_mask, save_mask and write_recrop operations live in spacr.qt.mask_engine. Keep the image-mask pairing and provenance with your curated training data. Use the linked API and training lessons when moving from a reviewed example to a reproducible workflow.
